Code 
#Import the Data 
drugdata<-read.csv("drug_spending-1.csv")
view(drugdata)

Introduction

Exploring the percentage of GDP allocated to healthcare and pharmaceutical spending in different countries over time is very interesting and essential for many different reasons. To begin with, because we are looking at percent GDP, we can look at any country regardless of its financial situation. Looking at percent GDP increases awareness of the efficiency of healthcare systems and economic implications, allowing the governments of the world to allocate their resources more effectively. Looking at different countries and their spending offers a comparison to potentially improve healthcare spending. Additionally, it helps assess the impact of healthcare policies and understanding the relationship between economic growth and healthcare. On top of that, observing healthcare expenses is essential for global health security, and can help identify countries with better resources and who is better equipped to respond to a global health crisis. Overall, analyzing healthcare spending provides insights for policy-making and healthcare management.

In this project, we are exploring the percent GDP spent in a given year between the years of 1970 to 2015 in countries that focused more of their spending on pharmaceuticals and what this reveals about their healthcare system. We will also be calculating the percent change of those countries. Finally, we will be comparing the percent GDP to the percent health spending out of all of the countries. The countries we are going to be focusing on are Portugal, Korea, Sweden, Norway, Great Britain, Finland, Germany, Belgium, Iceland, and France. We decided to focus on those countries because they were the only countries that had data from 1970 to 2015. Our data came from the “Pharmaceutical Drug Spending by countries” dataset on Data Hub. Data Hub got their information from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development. In this project, the variables we will be exploring include percent GDP, country, year, and percent of health spending. We hypothesize that because the countries mentioned above focus more of their spending on healthcare, from 1970 onwards their percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals should increase.

Results

Code 
drugdata1 <- drugdata
drugdata1$LOCATION <- drugdata1$LOCATION %>%
  fct_recode("Belgium" = "BEL",
              "Germany" = "DEU",
              "Korea" = "KOR",
              "Norway" = "NOR")
select_drug <-drugdata1 %>%
  filter(TIME != 2016) %>%
  filter(LOCATION %in% c("Belgium", "Germany", "Korea", "Norway"))

select_drug %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = TIME, y = PC_GDP/100, color = LOCATION, linetype = LOCATION)) +
  geom_line() +
   labs(title = "The Top and Bottom 2 Countries in Percent of GDP spent \n on Pharmaceuticals in the Year 1970 Plotted Over Time to 2015", tag = "Figure 1")+
  xlab("Years") +
  ylab("Percent of GDP Spent \n on Pharmaceuticals") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_size(guide = "none") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format())

Figure 1: As seen on the graph throughout the time period of 1970 to 2015 all the selected countries experienced a positive increase in the percent of GDP spent on pharmaceuticals over time. Korea had the largest increase visualized, growing almost ~200%! We selected the top and bottom 2 percent GDP spenders in 1970 to provide a stark contrast which is very visible. Between the years of 1990 and ~2002 is the time period of the greatest increase in GDP spending for the four countries selected as the slopes of the lines seem to be greatest/steepest between these years. The lines are not only in different types of colors but also dashes as a way to accommodate those who may be color blind or printing in black & white.

Code 
percentDiff <- drugdata %>%
  filter(TIME == 1970 | TIME == 2015) %>%
  filter(LOCATION %in% c("GBR", "SWE", "PRT", "NOR", "KOR", "ISL", "DEU", "FRA", "FIN", "BEL")) %>%
  select("LOCATION", "TIME", "PC_GDP") %>%
  group_by(LOCATION) %>%
  summarize(percentdiff= (max(PC_GDP)/min(PC_GDP))*100) %>%
  arrange(desc(percentdiff))
  
  


percentDiff$LOCATION <- percentDiff$LOCATION %>%
  fct_recode("Belgium" = "BEL",
              "Finland" = "FIN",
              "France" = "FRA",
              "Germany" = "DEU",
              "Iceland" = "ISL",
              "Korea" = "KOR",
              "Norway" = "NOR",
              "Portugal" = "PRT",
              "Sweden" = "SWE",
              "Great Britian" = "GBR")

  


tablediff <- percentDiff %>%
  kbl(col.names = c("Location", "Percent Change (%)"), digits = 2, caption = "Figure 2 Comparing Countries Percent Change of Percent GDP\\\\Spent on Pharmaceuticals from 1970 to 2015") %>%
  kable_paper()

Code 
percentDiff$LOCATION <- fct_reorder(percentDiff$LOCATION, percentDiff$percentdiff, max)


percentDiff %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=LOCATION, y=percentdiff/100)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Comparing Countries Percent Change of Percent GDP \n Spent on Pharmaceuticals from 1970 to 2015", tag = "Figure 2.1", caption = "Only countries with complete data from the year 1970 to 2015 were subsetted to provide consistent comparisons \n (ie Canada having data collected for 1970 but not for 2015 was excluded)") +
  xlab("Country") +
  ylab("Percent Change from 1970 to 2015") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))

Figure 2 & 2.1: This graph shows the percent change of percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals from the years of 1970 to 2015. The countries in the figures were the only countries with data from 1970 to 2015. This figure helps visualize the percent change in GDP to see what countries invested more of their spending on drugs or pharmaceuticals. The graph is in ascending order to make it easier to visualize. It is interesting to see that Portugal’s percent change was much greater than other countries during this time period. In figure 1 we observed Korea’s increase in percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals was very large and to see that Portugal’s is greater puts into perspective how much more the country as a whole spends on drugs compared to what they have in the past.

Code 
drugdata_Avg <- drugdata %>%
  group_by(LOCATION)%>%
  summarise(avg_PC_HEALTHXP = mean(PC_HEALTHXP), 
            avg_PC_GDP = mean(PC_GDP),avg_TOTAL_SPEND = mean(TOTAL_SPEND)) %>%
  mutate(select_location = case_when(LOCATION %in% c("BEL", "FIN", "FRA", "DEU", "ISL", "KOR", "NOR", "PRT",  "SWE", "GBR", "USA") ~ LOCATION, TRUE ~ NA))
  
ggplot(drugdata_Avg, aes(x = avg_PC_GDP/100, 
                     y = avg_PC_HEALTHXP/100, size= avg_TOTAL_SPEND, color = avg_TOTAL_SPEND)) +
  geom_point() +
  ggtitle("Exploring the trend between Percent GDP and Percent of Health", subtitle =  "Spending on Pharmaceuticals using their respective Averages by country")+
  labs(tag = "Figure 3", caption = "Average Total Pharmaceutical Spending is also represented by the size of the points to visulize\n the data without relying on color. This graph contains data all thoughout 1970 - 2016 because\n for some countries the data collection has inconsitancies for example some countries data\n starts at a later year and there are random missing years where data was not collected") + 
  xlab("Average Percent of GDP Spent \n on Pharmaceuticals") +
  ylab("Average Percent of Health Spending \n on Pharmaceuticals") +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se= FALSE, col="darkgray", linetype="dashed")+
  geom_label_repel(aes(label=select_location), min.segment.length=0, box.padding=1, size = 4, segment.color="black")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_size(guide = "none") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 10), legend.title = element_text(angle = 270, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 0.5), plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "right", legend.box.just = "center") +
  scale_color_continuous(name = "Average Total Pharmaceutical Spending", type = "gradient", label = label_comma(), guide = guide_colourbar(direction = "vertical", title.position = "right")) +
  stat_cor(p.accuracy = 0.001, r.accuracy = 0.01)

Figure 3: As seen on the graph, most countries display a linear relationship between the average percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals and the average percent of health spending on pharmaceuticals. A linear relationship between the two variables displayed in the graph by the dashed line of best fit and the R value being moderately close to 1 which indicates that countries tend to allot a proportional amount of their healthcare budgets to pharmaceuticals making a relatively strong linear relationship. The p-value being so small (p<0.001) means that the linear relationship between “Average Percent of GDP Spent on Pharmaceuticals” and “Average Percent of Health Spending on Pharmaceuticals” is statistically significant, meaning that it is likely not chance that these two variables have a linear correlation. The only country that does not follow relatively linear relationship is the United States. On average, the United States spends a large portion of its budget on pharmaceuticals, however it does not make up a large quantity of healthcare spending. The total spending on drugs by the USA is also visualized by the large dot and bright blue color but this only accentuates its abnormality.

Discussion

This project aimed to observe the percent change of different countries’ percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals and healthcare. To make the figures more accessible, we visualized the graphs by color and by different line types to accommodate for color blindness or people viewing these figures in black and white.The first graph confirmed our hypothesis that in the time period of 1970 to 2015, all selected countries showcased an increase in the percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals. As seen in figure 1, Korea had an impressive increase in pharmaceutical spending in the late 90s and early 2000s. This could imply that Korea decided to be more healthcare focused and take better care of their citizens’ health. The first table shows the percent differences of pharmaceutical spending from the first year (1970) to the last year (2015). Interestingly enough, Korea had the second highest percent difference, following Portugal. The second graph is just a bar graph of the table to visually see the percent difference between the selected countries. The final graph (figure …) compares the average percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals and the average percent of healthcare spending on pharmaceuticals of all of the countries in the dataset. All of the selected countries followed a fairly linear trend, except for the United States. The United States spends a large percent of its GDP on pharmaceuticals, but it does not make up a large quantity of healthcare. For example, the US may spend their money on other aspects of healthcare, like surgeries.

The data collection from Data Hub may not have been consistent because the data came from many different sources as they were combined to form this one dataset. Additionally, there was no clear indication of how the data were collected from any of the sources so we must assume that they were collected using the same methods and are uniform. We are also assuming that the data were collected in a random and unbiased manner. Another limitation is that some countries did not have data from the years 1970-2015. For example, Israel only had data from 2000 to 2015. There were some gaps in the years, which meant that we couldn’t look at every country in the dataset’s percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals over time.

Understanding that we both are not experts on pharmaceutical policy and how the spending amount of a given country effects the people’s health or well-being. We can only analyze the data how it has been presented to us. When graphing the Average Percent of GDP Spent on Pharmaceuticals vs Average Percent of Health Spending on Pharmaceuticals on diagram 3 it can be seen that the USA is the only country to not follow the general linear trend this may be because the USA could be spending their healthcare budget on other things like surgeries or doctors visits. After further investigation into the dataset the United States is the only country surveyed to not provide universal health care for its citizens this could explain why the United States has such a disproportionate spending on drugs as compared to the other countries because citizens of the US probably opt for the cheaper fix to a medical problem in drugs than the expensive surgery that could cure the person that would otherwise be covered by universal insurance in other countries. Therefore for the USA to join the general trend observed in figure 3 I believe they would have to implement Universal Healthcare. As seen in figure one Korea had such a large spike in percent GDP spent on pharmaceuticals in the 1990’s through the early 2000’s and after some background research Korea implemented universal healthcare in 1989 so that could be a direct causation that the graph visualized. Moreover the countries that we analyzed lie very close to the line of the best (exception being Korea) but overall it can be determined that the spending on pharmaceuticals of the USA is in stark contrast with those countries who provide universal healthcare so we believe that the US should convert their policies to provide as such services.
